name: Vitamin B12 cream

lead: Vitamin B12 cream is a topical product containing cobalamin, sold for eczema (atopic dermatitis). People with eczema-prone skin use it to reduce redness, itch and rough patches so the skin looks calmer and more even.

A handful of clinical trials in atopic dermatitis exist, including a randomised placebo-controlled multicentre trial published in 2004 and a 2017 left-to-right comparison against a standard emollient.

paras: The cream is applied to affected skin as a moisturiser-style product, often as an alternative or complement to standard emollients. Some formulations use liposomes to help the vitamin cross the skin.

Topical B12 is generally treated as low-risk. B12 in general is well tolerated per Wikipedia, with allergy to cobalt a reason it is not recommended. Skin that does not improve is usually reviewed by a dermatologist.

chain: Reduced itch and redness (proposed nitric oxide scavenging)
angle.text: Eczema-prone users apply B12 cream to lessen redness and itch. The visual benefit comes from calmer skin rather than any anti-ageing effect.

lead: Vitamin B12 cream is a topical preparation containing cobalamin, the vitamin otherwise taken orally or by injection.[1] Its main appearance-related use is for eczema, where reducing inflammation and dryness leaves skin looking smoother and less red.

The 2004 randomised, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial by Stücker and colleagues in the British Journal of Dermatology evaluated topical B12 in atopic dermatitis; the work was motivated by B12's ability to scavenge nitric oxide, which is implicated in itch and redness.[2] A 2017 randomised left-to-right trial by Nistico and colleagues compared a vitamin B12 barrier cream with a glycerol-petrolatum emollient and reports it as superior in its title.[2] A 2011 paper described a liposomal cobalamin hydrogel, noting B12 is light-sensitive and poorly permeable through skin.[2]

paras: B12 exists in oral, injectable and nasal forms; cyanocobalamin is the most air-stable and is common in pharmaceutical preparations.[1] In topical products it is formulated into creams, sometimes with liposomes.[2]

PubMed lists a randomised placebo-controlled multicentre trial of topical B12 in atopic dermatitis (Stücker et al., 2004), a randomised left-to-right comparison of a B12 barrier cream against a standard emollient (Nistico et al., 2017), and a liposomal cobalamin hydrogel study (Jung et al., 2011).[2] A 2013 review of integrative approaches noted that studies had not yet shown improvement in atopic dermatitis with vitamin or mineral supplements taken orally.[2]
B12 is generally well tolerated; the main caution Wikipedia lists is cobalt allergy.[1]
